rationale: B wins because it does the same four-angle map as A but finds the sharper reporting holes faster. “Perplexity will pay publishers it cites. It won't say how much.” is cleaner and more editor-ready than A's slightly padded “Perplexity offers publishers a revenue cut after months of legal threats over its content use.” A is good; B is better at saying what the reporter will actually ask first.
gaps_in_A: “after months of legal threats” invents a timeline the update does not provide. The facts say criticism and legal threats happened, not how long they lasted.
“Not for trade commerce press cheering the launch” is a lazy caricature of a beat. Say who it is not for without pretending every trade reporter is a cheerleader.
The funding angle asks for “any revenue figure, take-rate, or margin” but does not ask the harder publisher-side question B catches: whether there is meaningful ad revenue to share today.
The set is strong, but several sections are over-explained. The material is there; it occasionally reads like it is trying to prove it did the homework.
gaps_in_B: “takes a referral fee on every sale” overstates the fact pattern. The update says Perplexity earns a referral fee; it does not say every sale carries one.
“the company's first structural answer to that fight” invents chronology. Maybe true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
“the first concrete monetization signal since the raise” is another unsupported first. Do not smuggle in history the update did not give you.
“Perplexity will pay publishers it cites” is punchy but broad. The fact is a revenue-sharing program when a publisher's article is used in an answer; participation and payouts are still holes.
